A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MCP research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V4 reports original Gaussian simulations and experiments using MNIST, SST-2, human-activity accelerometer data and CIFAR-100, including coverage and localization results.

after.justification: V5 retains original experiments and adds multiple-changepoint simulations, baseline comparisons, Cauchy experiments and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: V4 excludes n from candidate confidence sets and handles exchangeability through a separate pre-test. V5 incorporates the no-change candidate n into MCP and its output. New Section 6 also introduces a procedure that uses KCPD estimates to isolate intervals and applies MCP separately within them.

E1.justification: V5 adds a multiple-changepoint task and Cauchy location-change data. Gaussian, MNIST, SST-2, HAR and CIFAR-100 coverage is retained, including mixed sentiment changes. No-change data already appeared in v4's pre-test simulations; the new confidence-set analysis is not wholly new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: V5 Tables 2–3 add evaluated comparisons with Siegmund (1988) and Cho and Kirch (2022), whereas v4's Gaussian table compares MCP score variants. V4's fitted-mean Gaussian-score comparison disappears; v5's misspecified Gaussian score on Cauchy data is a different experiment.

E3.justification: V4's Gaussian table uses n=1000, changepoint 400 and three score variants. V5 Table 1 instead evaluates an oracle-score grid with n=100, 200 and 500, means ±δ for δ=1 or 2, and changepoint 2n/5. Additional protocols test boundary locations, combining rules, misspecified scores and multiple changepoints. V5 also reports applying the no-change test where v4 explicitly omitted subsequent pre-testing.

E4.justification: V5 adds boundary-location sensitivity (Figure 6), rejection-power profiles (Figure 7), sample-size and signal-strength sensitivity (Table 1), score misspecification under Cauchy data (Table 3), combining-rule comparisons (Table 4), and confidence-set behavior without a change (Table 5). The certified-MNIST analysis and matrix visualization are retained.

E5.justification: V4 reports uncertainty around coverage only. V5 additionally labels standard errors for width, bias and mean absolute deviation, and identifies coverage errors as binomial, generally at 95%. Figure 7 specifies 200 oracle runs and 10 KDE runs. Both versions state 1000 trials for their aggregate Gaussian tables; an overall increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: The Gaussian summary results are replaced and expanded, and multiple-change, baseline, robustness and no-change results are added. For example, v5 Table 3 reports Cauchy coverage of 0.97 for oracle MCP, 0.94 for Gaussian-score MCP, 0.12 for Siegmund and 0.82 for Cho–Kirch. The reported MNIST, SST-2, HAR and CIFAR-100 confidence sets remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 5.1 reverses the rank comparison from greater-than to less-than and adds an optimality claim over arbitrary level-alpha tests, with an additional proof paragraph. Lemma E.1, renamed F.1, receives substantive corrections to its CDF inequalities and equality-case argument. V5 also expands the confidence-set definition to include n and adds reasoning for the multiple-change extension.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same principal claims: broadly applicable MCP localization, finite-sample coverage under exchangeability, a conformal Neyman–Pearson result, and practical classifier-based applications. The added material does not substantively revise these summaries.

C2.justification: V5 explicitly discusses the tradeoff between MCP's broader assumptions and the sharper Gaussian intervals of specialized baselines, and explains robustness to Cauchy data and misspecified scores. It adds discussion of wide sets without a changepoint, leftward estimator bias and the heuristic nature of the multiple-change extension. It also corrects the empirical discussion's 'exactly' nominal coverage assertion to 'at least'.

D1.justification: V5 adds computational-cost statements, prefix/suffix class precomputation guidance, and the KCPD kernel and median-distance bandwidth specification. The code-access link, M1 Pro CPU, runtime claim, MNIST architecture and training procedure remain unchanged. These are limited additions to implementation documentation.

R1.justification: V5 expands positioning against classical nonparametric localization and confidence-set methods, adding discussion of Carlstein, Lee, Zou, Dümbgen and Siegmund. It also incorporates KCPD literature and Bhattacharya–Ramdas results on MCP consistency, substantially extending the theoretical and comparative context.

P1.justification: V5 reorganizes the method exposition and related work, moves the coverage theorem into a dedicated theoretical-results subsection, promotes Gaussian experiments from Appendix A to Section 7.1, and moves MNIST to Appendix A. It introduces per-anomaly versus per-candidate terminology and restructures the appendices.

P2.justification: V5 adds multiple-change, boundary and power plots and several new tables, while substantially restructuring the Gaussian results table. Figure 2 now displays left/right p-values instead of discrepancy statistics, retained displays are relocated, and the CIFAR sample-image time labels are corrected to changepoint 300.

improvement.justification: The new external baselines and sensitivity analyses address important empirical gaps in v4, while no-change integration and proof corrections are useful. However, v5 Table 1 reports coverage 0.47 for a 95% set and 0.94 for a 50% set at n=100, δ=1, contradicting its calibration discussion. The expanded Theorem 5.1 also claims arbitrary-test optimality without establishing that ordinary likelihood-ratio optimality transfers to its rank test. These unresolved issues in central evidence and theory prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
